title: Delhi Fire Calls Dip on Diwali With 214 Fire Incidents Reported Citywide
excerpt: Delhi Fire Service logged 257 calls on November 8, down from 269 last year, with fire calls easing from 231 to 214 — even as AIIMS treated 42 burn cases and air quality turned severe.
body:
• Delhi Fire Service received 257 calls on Diwali day, November 8, including 214 fire-related calls and 24 incidents linked to firecrackers.
  • Fire calls fell from 231 last year to 214 this year, and total calls eased from 269 to 257, a dip of about 4 percent.
  • The busiest window was 8 pm to 10 pm, when 85 calls came in, 84 of them fire-related.
  • AIIMS New Delhi treated 42 Diwali-related burn cases, including 11 patients with major burns.

NEW DELHI — Delhi recorded a quieter Diwali on the fire front this year, with the Delhi Fire Service (DFS) handling 257 calls on November 8, of which 214 were fire-related, according to official figures released on Monday. The total was down from 269 calls during the same period last year, while fire-related calls fell from 231 last year to 214 this year, DFS Chief A. K. Malik said at a media briefing on the department's preparedness and the incidents reported during the festival.

Of the day's fire calls, 24 incidents were linked to firecrackers, and the department also received one forest fire call, Malik said. He added that about 281 calls were recorded in the overnight window between 6 pm on Diwali evening and 6 am the following morning, with around 178 of them received by midnight. Six people sustained injuries in fire incidents, and around five fire personnel sustained minor injuries during firefighting operations, with none suffering serious injuries, he said.

The pressure peaked late in the evening. Between 8 pm and 10 pm, the service handled 85 emergency calls, 84 of them fire-related and eight specifically linked to cracker incidents, Chief Fire Officer Abhilash Kumar Malik confirmed. Another 61 calls followed between 10 pm and midnight, including 60 fire-related reports. Earlier in the day, 36 calls were recorded between 7 am and 2 pm, 27 between 2 pm and 6 pm, and 32 between 6 pm and 8 pm, before a quieter 16 incidents between midnight and 7 am. Crews were dispatched across the city to blazes in residential properties, a banquet hall, a godown and several industrial factories. Reported fires included two adjoining factories on Shamshan Ghat Wali Road in Nangli Sakrawati, a factory in the Narela Industrial Area and an NDMC godown beneath the Safdarjung Flyover.

Accounts differed on how the largest blazes should be labelled. ANI quoted Malik as saying seven major fire calls were received during the period, while a department officer told PTI that no major fire was reported — a difference that news summaries attributed to contrasting uses of the term "major." The department had deployed extra crews and quick-response teams across 71 stations ahead of Diwali.

Hospitals still saw a significant casualty load. The Department of Plastic, Reconstructive and Burns Surgery at AIIMS, New Delhi, reported 42 Diwali-related burn injury cases till 11 am on Monday. Of these, 11 patients suffered major burns, including four admitted to the Intensive Care Unit and seven to the ward, while the remaining 31 cases were categorised as minor burns. Five patients underwent surgery and eight remained admitted, including one critical patient. Six children below 10 years suffered burn injuries; the youngest patient was five years old, and an eight-year-old child with 45 percent burn surface area involvement was reported to be critical. The AIIMS report stated that 37 cases were related to firecracker burns, while two involved potash burns, including one involving a 13-year-old child.

The festival was held under green-cracker rules. The Delhi government had urged citizens to follow Supreme Court guidelines mandating that only CSIR-NEERI-certified "green" firecrackers could be sold, and only through designated outlets approved by the Delhi Police. The district magistrate for East Delhi limited the use of green crackers to between 6 am and 7 am and 8 pm and 10 pm on November 7 and 8, and bursting firecrackers was prohibited within 300 metres of sensitive locations such as hospitals, nursing homes, educational institutions and old-age homes, with joint enforcement teams of district officials and police patrolling for unauthorised sales and use. Despite the lower fire-call count, air quality still plunged after widespread firecracker use: the Central Pollution Control Board recorded an Air Quality Index of 406 at the ITO monitoring station at about 4:20 am on Monday, in the "severe" range.

nri_angle: For Indian families abroad who celebrated Diwali this weekend, Delhi's lower fire-call tally offers a concrete safety snapshot of how the festival passed in the capital this year.
